questions.prompt: Walk through everything POST /e does with a request between arrival and answer, naming every way it can say no: which status and error code each refusal gets, which headers come with it, the order the checks run in and why that order, and, for the three load-protection refusals, which ingest test pins each one down.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The credential comes first: no key in either the Bearer header or the ?k= query is a 401, an unknown or revoked key is also a 401, and a valid key used from an origin outside its allowed list is a 403, which separates 'who are you' from 'you may not send from there'.

[w3] Backpressure is checked before any per-request work: when the stream backlog is above the watermark the answer is 429 with Retry-After 2. Its test sets a watermark of 3, pushes five entries onto the in-memory stream and samples depth on every request, so the shed is deterministic.

[w3] The monthly quota has two thresholds: past the soft limit the request still gets 202 but carries an x-quota-state: soft header for the banner, and at the full allowance it is a 429 with code QUOTA_EXCEEDED and x-quota-state: hard. The test drives a mutable usage value through 100, 850 and 1000 of an allowance of 1000.

[w2] Shape errors are all-or-nothing: the body is parsed as one event or a bounded array, any invalid event raises a schema error for the whole request, and the error handler maps that to 400 VALIDATION; every other unexpected error becomes 500 INTERNAL with no detail leaked.

[w2] The rate limit is charged per event, not per request: a 3-event batch empties a bucket of capacity 3, after which even a single event gets 429 RATE_LIMITED. The tests freeze the limiter's clock at zero so no tokens refill mid-test.

[w2] The order is deliberate: identity and origin before anything that spends shared resources, so an anonymous caller cannot consume a project's quota reads or rate tokens; load-shedding and quota before parsing the body; and the body parsed before the rate limiter, because the bucket is debited by the real number of events in the request.

questions.prompt: Explain how Pulse keeps personal data and untrustworthy client timestamps out of what it ingests, starting from what the PII test actually asserts, and judge how far each protection really reaches: what slips past it, and what would you change?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Scrubbing happens before the event is queued, by a rule per property name: deny drops the property outright (password, ssn, credit_card, $ip_raw, authorization), hash replaces the value with a sha256 hex digest (email, phone, ip), and every other property passes through unchanged.

[w3] The test asserts what lands, not what a function returns: it posts a signup with password, email and plan, reads the entry back off the in-memory stream, and expects password gone, plan untouched and email replaced by a 64-character hex string that differs from the original.

[w2] The reach is top-level names only: matching is case-insensitive on each key of the property bag, but nested objects are not walked, so props.user.email or a key named user_email or emailAddress passes through readable. Walk nested values and match name patterns, or switch to an allowlist of known-safe properties.

[w2] An unsalted sha256 of an email pseudonymizes but does not anonymize: anyone holding a candidate list of addresses can hash it and match. A keyed hash (HMAC with a server secret) keeps values joinable and countable while blocking that dictionary match.

[w2] Server time is the authority for client timestamps: a client ts within 48 hours of ingest time is kept, one further out is clamped to the boundary and the event gets a $ts_clamped flag. An unparseable ts quietly becomes the ingest time with no flag, so that distortion stays invisible.

[w1] Credentials are kept out of logs as well as out of events: the beacon path carries the write key in ?k=, so the production request serializer passes every logged URL through redactKeyInUrl to strip that value first.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict the ingest edge's three load protections (the per-key rate limit, the backlog watermark and the monthly quota) as they would behave in production behind six ingest replicas. For each, say what its test proves, what it does not prove, and what you would change.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The rate limiter lives in each process's memory, so behind six replicas a project's effective rate is six times the configured one; the code accepts that for a guardrail and notes a shared Redis bucket would make it global. The frozen-clock test proves the bucket arithmetic on one instance, never the fleet-wide limit.

[w3] The quota counter is shared (a Redis key per project per calendar month), but it is read and then incremented separately, and the increment is fire-and-forget after the events are queued: concurrent requests near the limit all read 'under' and overshoot it, and a failed increment under-meters with nothing reported. A shared atomic check-and-increment (for example a Lua script) closes both gaps.

[w2] The watermark is a sampled number: each instance re-reads the backlog at most once a second and admits everything in between, and each replica samples on its own schedule. A test that samples on every request, as the backpressure test does, proves the threshold but not the sampling lag.

[w2] Retry-After is a fixed guess on two of the three refusals: 2 seconds for backpressure whatever the backlog, and an hour for a hard quota even though the allowance only resets with the calendar month, so a well-behaved client retries every hour for the rest of the month. Only the rate limit computes its value from the bucket's deficit.

[w2] Charging one token per event is fair, since an event is the unit of load, but a request whose event count exceeds the bucket's capacity can never be admitted, and its Retry-After still names a wait computed from the deficit. That is harmless only while the configured burst stays above the largest batch the schema allows.

[w1] Abuse visibility is per instance too: the per-key allowed and rejected counters sit in the same in-memory limiter and the ops endpoint lists them sorted by rejections, so on-call has to merge six lists to see one abuser.

[w1] Quotas meter what was accepted, never what was stored: billing from stored counts would under-bill whenever the pipeline loses events and hide the loss, so the number the customer saw accepted is the number charged.
